title: Most engaging images mix simply describable and indescribable features

fields.label: Label
fields.value: Most engaging images mix simply describable and indescribable features

fields.label: Statement
fields.value: People tend to lose interest in images with no simple features (such as perfectly random ones), and the images that hold attention and seem most aesthetically pleasing are those in which some features are simple to describe while others have no short description findable by human visual perception.

fields.label: Chapter
fields.value: Ch. 10: Processes of Perception and Analysis

fields.label: Quotation
fields.value: the images that draw us in the most—and typically that we find the most aesthetically pleasing—are those for which some features are simple for us to describe, but others have no short description that can be found by any of our standard processes of visual perception.

fields.label: Agent
fields.value: delphisci A New Kind of Science claim extractor

fields.label: Assumptions
fields.value: Stephen Wolfram, A New Kind of Science (Champaign, IL: Wolfram Media, 2002), Chapter 10, “Processes of Perception and Analysis”; section “Defining Complexity” (from p. 557), p. 559. Scope: human visual attention and aesthetic preference for images

fields.label: Assessment
fields.value: GPT-5.6 Sol on wolfram2002-ch10-07: partially-resolvable, resolvability 0.54

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: Public behavioral and imaging studies can test restricted versions of the predicted preference. The precise mixture of describable and indescribable features usually must be reconstructed with debatable proxies.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: For images independently scored on computable simple structure and residual incompressibility, model viewing time, return choices, and aesthetic ratings. An inverted-U preference with low ratings for both fully predictable and featureless random images supports the claim.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
Existing datasets may not span the required controlled image continuum.

Human-findable description length is not directly measured.

Aesthetic preference varies by person and culture.

fields.label: Dimension scores
fields.value:
data adequacy: 0.42
analysis feasibility: 0.6
operationalizability: 0.62
discriminating power: 0.48
data existence: 0.6

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: Intermediate-complexity preference is a known empirical question, and looking time is a measurable variable. Existing public materials do not line up with the specific contrast among random images, simply patterned images, and images whose features split into describable and indescribable. The claim is testable in part through related studies and is not settled by one open dataset.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Classify images by whether human observers have a short description of some features but not others, then measure looking time and preference against purely random and purely simple controls. Preference peaking on the mixed class would support the claim; equal or higher preference for random or purely simple images would refute it.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
Aesthetic preference and attention are task-dependent, and 'aesthetically pleasing' has several competing scales.

No single public dataset uses Wolfram's partition into simply describable versus indescribable features.

analysis feasibility: 0.4
discriminating power: 0.46
